short: No earlier sentence-level lipreading study used a CTC decoder, and the field took this one up; the comparisons break: an 86.4% word-level HMM baseline, a 10-minute panel, silent dictation untested.
position: LipNet [@assael2016lipnet] changes one component, the decoder (M06): spatiotemporal convolutions, Bi-GRUs and a character CTC loss in one model. That is ahead of the field: of the 67 sentence-level lip-reading studies first public before it, 41 name hidden Markov models and none a CTC or attention decoder, and the only [concurrent] study with a spatiotemporal front end reports its 3D variants as worse than its 2D ones [@chung2016lrw]; the field then took both, and the best GRID result in the wiki still uses a 3D front end [@xue2026linprovsr]. The headline comparisons do not hold: the 86.4% "state-of-the-art" is a video-only accuracy from speaker-dependent word HMMs decoded with the full GRID grammar [@gergen2016turbo], so the 2.8x claim crosses task level, split and decoder constraint, and the "experienced human lipreaders" are three hearing-impaired students given ten minutes of annotated video (4.2). Silent dictation is the named application although every utterance is overtly spoken, a transfer cost measured in lip video since 2010 [@florescu2010silent], so M04 is behind; and no Table 2 number carries a seed or an interval, while the study reimplemented as its LSTM baseline reports both [@wand2016lipreading]. The protocol it defined (M12) is its second lasting contribution, now followed by 54 unseen-speaker and 41 overlapped-speaker GRID studies.
